Abstract—Quantum Key Distribution relies on the principles
of quantum mechanics to offer highly secure key exchange

of quantum mechanics to offer highly secure key exchange
against eavesdropping. Channel noise and device imperfections,
especially in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum environments,
have a great impact on current protocol performance, such as
BB84. Noise-aware simulation and optimization for the BB84
protocol on the IBM Qiskit platform are presented in this
paper. A realistic depolarizing noise model is used to simulate
quantum channel noise, and the Quantum Bit Error Rate is

quantum channel noise, and the Quantum Bit Error Rate is
characterized in different noise probabilities. The approach here
allows us to test and optimize QKD performance in realistic
NISQ-based implementations and gives a description of the
protocol robustness in real operating conditions. Experimental
results show the influence of noise on the rates of key generation
and confirm the feasibility of the proposed framework for secure
and scalable quantum communications.

and scalable quantum communications.
Index Terms —Quantum Key Distribution, BB84 Protocol;
Depolarizing Noise, Quantum Bit Error Rate, Quantum Com-
munication, Noise-Aware Optimization, Qiskit Simulation.
I. I NTRODUCTION
The rapid evolution of communication technologies has
made the secure data carriage a major requirement in some
specific spheres of finance, healthcare, defense, and govern-
ment. The development of quantum computing also poses

ment. The development of quantum computing also poses
a challenge of eliminating such conventional methods as
quantum algorithms, including the Shor algorithm, can factor
numbers of large sizes in a only a number of steps, thereby
posing a threat to effectively breaking most popular public-
key algorithms. The imminent security threat has facilitated
the quantization efforts of Quantum Key Distribution which
represents a paradigm fundamental of quantum mechanics

represents a paradigm fundamental of quantum mechanics
with the aim of offering secure communication channels.
The QKD protocol which has been used most extensively,
and in reality been the most successful is the protocol named
BB84, constituted in 1984 by Bennett and Brassard. Contrary
to the other conventional key exchange protocols, the security
of BB84 is not assured due to the mathematical complexity but
on the principles of quantum physics i.e. the superposition of

on the principles of quantum physics i.e. the superposition of
states and no-cloning of quantum states and disturbance caused
by measurements. In the BB84 protocol, qubits are exchanged
between two parties (Alice and Bob) with the help of alternate
bases to finally retrieve a shared secret key. The error in the
key as a result of unavoidable measurement perturbation can
identify the eavesdropper (Eve) hence providing a security
against eavesdropping. Now that quantum simulation models

against eavesdropping. Now that quantum simulation models
have grown in recent years, such as Qiskit, researchers can
now deploy and experiment with QKD protocols in realistic
conditions i.e. with noise and decoherence. The security of
BB84 implemented as a parameters such as the Quantum
Bit Error Rate by simulating realistic imperfections. The
project targets the implementation of the BB84 protocol using
Qiskit and its functionality on its implementation on noisy

Qiskit and its functionality on its implementation on noisy
environments, as well as proving its usefulness as a secure
cryptographic tool in the era of the quantum computers.
Unlike previous works, this paper provides a comparative
analysis of the BB84 protocol in realistic models of noise in
the field of quantum computation, namely depolarizing noise,
amplitude damping noise, and phase noise. Based on these
models, conclusions have been made regarding the robustness
of the protocol.

of the protocol.

The qubits represent each a potential key bit and the
encoding of keys depends on the random selection of the
basis by Alice and the random choice of the value of the

which experiences the real world imperfections of depolarizing
noise, loss of photons or errors in the devices and hence incurs
possible perturbation of the states sent.Bob then measures the

possible perturbation of the states sent.Bob then measures the
qubits in randomly chosen bases. Since quantum mechanics
is probabilistic, by the same basis in which Bob measures
Alice he will get the same value as Alice with a very high
probability. However, in case the bases are not equal, it
becomes random and such results cannot be directly used to
acquire the final key. In order to get the valid key bits, Alice
and Bob mutually exchange through a Classical Channel, we

and Bob mutually exchange through a Classical Channel, we
have the bases publicly announced (although not the actual
bits values) on which they have used to share a qubit. The
protocol operation known as key sifting, implies that the bits
in which both have utilized the same basis will be retained
to the raw key, the filtered key will then be analyzed with
the use of Quantum Bit Error Rate Analysis, which is the
measurement of the proportion of bits between Alice and Bob

measurement of the proportion of bits between Alice and Bob
that have been mismatched. When QBER is low, then the
channel is assured to be secure whereas high QBER can mean
that there is a substantial amount of noise in the channel or
that there is a channel eavesdropper. When QBER is large
then Alice and Bob can make additional error correction
and privacy amplification to retrieve the safe final key. The
method gives evidence of the resilience of the BB84 protocol

method gives evidence of the resilience of the BB84 protocol
to eavesdropping and provides a viable foundation to design
quantum communication with noisy channels.

Fig 2 plot shows the QBER vs probability of depolarizing
noise in BB84 Quantum Key Distribution. At zero noise
probability, as observed the QBER is also zero meaning at this
point, there is no error in transmission of qubits. The better the
chance of noise, the higher the QBER, which demonstrates the

and therefore, the protocol is resilient to small imperfections

value of about 0.15-0.20) is reached, which means that QKD
is vulnerable to high noise. This illustrates the application

Comparison with E91 and B92 Protocols
Schemes like E91 and B92 exhibit distinct performance
characteristics, the BB84 protocol remains the most widely
implemented QKD protocol. The E91 protocol uses entangled
photon pairs and Bell inequality tests, thus it provides very
strong eavesdropping detection at the price of requiring com-
plex entanglement sources. In turn, the B92 protocol uses only

plex entanglement sources. In turn, the B92 protocol uses only
two non-orthogonal states, offering simpler implementation at
the cost of significantly higher noise susceptibility, while the
system allows for substantially lower levels of eavesdropping-
induced disturbances compared to BB84. A more realistic
depolarizing noise model and the assessment of QBER un-
der operating conditions using NISQ are integrated into the
proposed noise-aware BBP84 optimization approach, allowing

proposed noise-aware BBP84 optimization approach, allowing
operational performance tuning without entanglement or sim-
plification of the protocol. This guarantees better scalability
and robustness compared to B92, and broader deployability
compared to E91, which constitutes the novelties in integrating
realistic noise modelling and optimization into BBP84-based
QKD implementations.

Limitations
The proposed noise-aware BB84 simulation framework pro-
vides valuable insights into QKD’s performance in realistic
NISQ environments for the depolarizing noise model used in
this study is an idealized approximation of practical quantum

this study is an idealized approximation of practical quantum
channels. Real systems often include additional noise sources
such as photon loss, detector dark counts and polarization
drift. The simulations are performed using Qiskit’s NISQ-
oriented backend and thus imperfectly model long-distance
optical fiber or free-space channels; this limits the direct trans-
ferability of the results to large-scale network deployments.
The BB84 protocol is considered; the framework does not

The BB84 protocol is considered; the framework does not
yet include adaptive or device-independent variants of QKD,
which may offer improved robustness. Future work will extend
the model to include more realistic channel characteristics,
multiple protocol families, and implementation-level security
considerations.
